Short answer: not quite — and the distinction matters.

A Bayesian 95% credible interval (CrI) and a frequentist p-value are answering different questions, and you can't directly translate one into the other.

What your output actually tells you

The coefficient of 0.45 with 95% CrI [0.12, 0.79] means: given your model and your data, there is a 95% probability that the true parameter lies between 0.12 and 0.79. That is a posterior probability statement about the parameter itself.

A frequentist p < 0.05 means: if the null hypothesis (β = 0) were true, the probability of observing data at least as extreme as yours is less than 5%. That is a statement about hypothetical repeated sampling, not about the parameter.

Why you cannot simply say 'p < 0.05'

The fact that your 95% CrI excludes zero does not make it equivalent to p < 0.05. This analogy is imprecise and will draw methodological criticism. Reviewers familiar with Bayesian methods will flag the conflation.

What you should report instead

Report the Bayesian quantities directly:
> The posterior estimate for the effect was 0.45 (95% CrI [0.12, 0.79]).

If you want a Bayesian-native directional summary, compute the probability of direction — P(β > 0 | data) — via bayestestR::pd(fit). With the full posterior above zero, P(β > 0 | data) will be very high (likely > 0.99). Report it as: '99% of the posterior mass was above zero.' This is a legitimate Bayesian directional claim, not a p-value.

Recommended language: 'The posterior median effect was 0.45 (95% CrI [0.12, 0.79]), with [X]% of the posterior mass above zero.'
